A Daughter’s Powerful Memoir Traces Her Relationship With Her Father And His Journey Of Gender Transition

September 14, 2026September 8, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 11:47
Instaread

Author and educator Tami Lou Castillo grew up with an unreliable father who was often absent for days at a time. She hoped that he would one day become the parent she needed, but there were only brief periods of happiness.

Her father Roy spent his life creating moulds for beautiful things yet was never able to do the same for himself. Thirty years later, Tami discovered the secret he kept hidden: her father, Roy, is now Connie. Connie is a woman finally comfortable in her own skin, after sixty years in the wrong body. Roy was one of the first people in California to have their name and gender changed on a birth certificate.

Tami is now sharing her story in a powerful new memoir titled ‘The Mould Maker’ (Hembury Books), out now. It is the story of a daughter’s search for her authentic father and the unconditional love that shapes us all, if only we allow it.

In a recent interview with us, Tami shared more about what it meant to learn about her father being a trans woman, how her own complicated relationship with Roy added complexity, and the humanity she hopes to bring to an increasingly hostile global conversation about the trans community.

Can you first tell us the emotional process for you going back through childhood memories to write ‘The Mould Maker’?

I actually used my emotions as a starting point when writing each chapter of The Mould Maker. I started with the memories that I’d always wanted to write about. Each of these memories became a chapter. For each chapter I zeroed in on the feeling associated with this particular memory, then I went to my favourite books to find a passage that resembled the same feeling of my memory. I typed a quote from that passage at the top of the page and used this quote as a container to shape and hold the writing.

I circled back to the meaning of the quote at the end of the chapter. For me, this tied the chapter into a coherent piece. So, my generative writing started with the feeling of each scene I wrote about. I repeated this approach for every chapter I wrote for The Mould Maker. During the editing process, I eventually took all the quotes out. What I found is that by removing the quote I was no longer relying on the quote to communicate my idea, but made me hone my writing more clearly and specifically to my own experience.

The emotional process of writing The Mould Maker overall was one of healing and gained understanding because when you write about your past, you get to revisit it through your current lived experience. This allows you to see it through the distance of time and learned wisdom. For me, this allowed me to see memories from a different point of view where I learned something new. You relive it, but not as the person you were at the time. I feel like I understand my life a lot more and have a more open acceptance and appreciation of my experiences. Its allowed me to open my heart more fully.

What prompted you to write this book now? 

It was Connie’s passing that prompted me to write my memoir. The whole process of writing TMM took me ten years. However, the impetus to tell Connie’s story didn’t hit me until Connie had passed away in 2015. It was only then I could see the full impact of her life on me and others who knew her (family and friends). A few months after she’d passed was when an aha moment came and I realized that I could fulfill a lifelong desire to write about my life and tell Connie’s story.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Tami Lou Castillo (@tamiloucastilloauthor)

Sharing the story of your transgender parent and Connie’s journey at a time when there wasn’t as much knowledge or information about the trans community as there is now, what were some of the biggest things you learned? 

When I started writing about Connie’s story, it was decades after she came out as trans. Even so, she came out in the 90’s and there was no information out in the world in terms of support, explanation, terms (the word transgender did not exist then), or accessible knowledge. There was no internet. Still, I had heard of this before  – that there were people in the world who felt like they were the other gender (the word sex was used back then).

It was a vague or taboo topic that was never discussed openly in society. At the time when Connie came out, I told less than a handful of friends because I’m not sure I understood it myself and there was a shame I felt because it was a taboo topic. I understood the basic premise of my dad’s dilemma – that my dad felt like she was female since childhood and that it was a lifelong issue that she was born with and it was never going to go away.

So, I knew that Connie was born this way and that living as a male had hindered her whole life – I experienced the evidence of this for years. Writing The Mould Maker gave me the opportunity to learn beyond a shadow of doubt that biology isn’t perfect, that genetics are not perfect, that Connie was born this way, and that there’s an essential need in every one of us to live authentically as who we inherently feel we are (our unique identity). Through taking the time to write about my life with my parent as my Dad, then as Connie, I learned the most important gift we have in life is unconditional love.

If we can love unconditionally, we will hold within us the most beautiful of gifts we have to offer. Unconditional love goes beyond boundaries, boxes, labels and judgements. This was the biggest lesson I learned through writing ‘The Mould Maker’. 

We are seeing global conversations around gender identity and even attacks on the trans community, often fueled by political culture wars as a distraction from real issues. What do you hope your memoir will allow people to think about amidst all of this? 

It’s quite disheartening to see the politicizing, shaming and hate-mongering of trans people. What I hope people will think from reading TMM is that every human being carries the same basic needs – to be seen and accepted for who we are – to be loved. Humans are not gatekeepers to other humans to determine what humans are more human than another.

Each one of us deserves to be loved and accepted as a human being. We are all worthy despite how we may look or appear. It’s our behaviors that need policing to maintain civil society, not our state of being. Gender identity is a state of being. I hope TMM shows that all of us humans are worthy of love and acceptance as we are.

As you share your memoir with a variety of audiences of all generations, what have been the most memorable or impactful conversations and reactions you’ve had so far? 

It is still early days since my memoir was released. But I have heard many times from readers who’ve told me they laughed and cried and felt like they lived the experience with me – this response has been the quite impactful because if they felt what I felt then they might also see that Connie, a transgender person, deserved all the sweetest things life has to offer as any of us.

If my readers feel that way about Connie, then I’ve accomplished what I’ve set out to do – to show that trans people are just people too, like me and you. The most impactful feedback I’ve received is from two people I know who read my book and both told me that reading my memoir made them want to be a better human. The only thing I can imagine better than that is all of us striving to be better humans.

The next most impactful feedback I’ve received is about me as a writer. One thing that has bowled me over is how many people have said my memoir is a page-turner and that they couldn’t put it down, that it’s ‘a beautifully told story’ and someone even described my writing as ‘masterful storytelling’.

For me, personally, I’ve had imposter syndrome the whole time I’ve been writing and, still, after my memoir was released. So, I’ve been pleasantly shocked to hear readers say this about my writing. Its touched me deeply and has encouraged me.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Tami Lou Castillo (@tamiloucastilloauthor)

Have your family read the book? If so, how have they reacted? 

My mom read about half of the book before she passed away recently. My younger brother, step-brother and step-sister have read it and my older brother and sister are looking forward to reading it. The ones that have read it liked it very much and felt like I got it right with interactions and portrayals of our lives.

What do you think is missing from many of the click-bait debates or news media conversations about the trans community?

Nuance and depth is missing. I find most of these conversations are conflated into Either and Ors or Black and Whites, so generalizations. Once you start generalizing, you have untruths and once untruths enter a conflated argument, you cannot arrive at understanding, only misunderstanding.

Essentially the human condition is not simple, its complex. Any media coverage that conflates trans topics into simple arguments or click-bait statements lose the opportunity to understand something complex and lose an opportunity to learn more about what it means to be human. Conflated debates or arguments perpetuate stereotypes and misunderstandings.

How can personal storytelling like ‘The Mould Maker’ become a source of healing or perspective-shifting in such a divided world?

I think personal story-telling may be the only way to shift perspectives in a divided world. It’s only when you can hear and feel someone’s truth that can change your own mind about previous notions you might hold. This rings true for me and for most people I know. When I hear someone’s story about something I previously misunderstood or was ignorant about, it’s only then I actually learn and take on board new knowledge and gain wisdom – when I learn from someone’s personal experience.

We learn from the truth of others. It what resonates with us – a person’s truth. It’s how we have learned since the beginning of humankind, through the sharing of our stories. So, it is my hope that sharing my personal truth with the rest of the world will heal misunderstandings of what it means to be a trans person and shift any perspectives that trans people are less than any other human being. 

There is so much compassion that comes through the pages of your book and it is very inspiring. How can each of us practice compassion today even in the midst of struggles? 

Thank you so much for saying this. I think it’s always a challenge in the midst of our own struggles to show compassion. What I always try to do (but not always succeed in the moment) is to put myself into another person’s shoes and try to look at the situation through their perspective and their feelings. When I do this, empathy and compassion bubble to the surface pretty quickly. The more we practice it, the more it becomes second nature.

You can order a copy of ‘The Mould Maker’, out now. Learn more about Tami Lou Castillo’s work on her website, and follow her on Instagram and Facebook.
